result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**`git merge`** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has two parents. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C---F---G      main
     \           \
      D---E-------M    feature (after `git merge main`)
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits one by one on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. The result is a straight line, as if you had started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C---F---G              main
                 \
                  D'---E'      feature (after `git rebase main`)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved exactly, with branch points visible | Rewritten to be linear |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for every replayed commit |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit, possibly several times |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No |
| Undo | Revert or reset the merge commit | Reset to the old tip via `git reflog` |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase local, unpushed work to tidy it up or catch up with `main` before opening a PR.
- Merge when integrating into a shared branch, or when the branch has already been pushed and others may have based work on it.
- Never rebase commits other people have pulled: their history will diverge from yours, and you would need a force push (`git push --force-with-lease`) to publish the rewritten branch.

A common workflow combines both: `git rebase main` on your feature branch to keep it current, then merge it into `main` when it is done.
